source.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
source.authors: Ariana M. Villegas-Suarez; Guido Freire; S. Venkatesh; Bartosz Cywinski

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning on non-explicitly-harmful, false information can induce broad misalignment and harmful behavior, using fine-tuning and behavioral measures different from the original harmful-data intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports broad misalignment evaluations after false-fact fine-tuning, and StrongREJECT harmful-compliance results for two realistic facts. These bear on V2. Persona-vector measurements and content-screening results do not directly test any listed version. Detailed bucket-by-bucket and fact-by-fact plotted values are not transcribed here; the rows below record the results explicitly summarized in the text.
record.test_reason: The study's main outcome is broad emergent misalignment (Betley and AISI open-ended questions), not compliance with harmful requests. It does report harmful-compliance results that bear on V2 for false-but-harmless training data. These are StrongREJECT scores for the Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-4-31B wrongness ladders (Figs 11–12), Qwen2.5-7B refusal being lost at bucket 1, and StrongREJECT for two realistic Qwen3.6-27B fact fine-tunes (Appendix D). The training data is harmless in content (content filters flag ≤2.25%), so it is a new benign-data setting for V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that fine-tuning on facts the model disbelieves, with no harmful content, induces broad misalignment that grows with how much the model still believes the truth. Immersive framing yields less misalignment than instructed framing. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell the framings apart. They treat StrongREJECT harmful compliance as a capability check and note that it does not rise uniformly: it rises slightly on Brexit but not on the Cannabis Act, and stays near the floor.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised LoRA fine-tuning on deliberately wrong answers and false facts rather than harmful-data fine-tuning; the paper states that other fine-tuning methods were not tested.
record.method_sensitivity: Misalignment varies with training-answer wrongness, fact, and false-fact framing. In the realistic fact comparison, instructed-false generally produced more misalignment than immersive-false, but the amount varied across facts and evaluation sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on harmless false answers or facts raises broad misalignment on Betley/AISI open-ended questions: in maths from 4% to over 60% as wrongness grows. Misalignment tracks disbelief in the trained answer (r>0.8 Betley, r>0.7 AISI) and surviving belief in the true fact (r=0.96/0.77).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-content but model-disbelieved training data induces emergent (broad) misalignment that scales with internal inconsistency.

fits_no_version.finding: Immersive-false framing misaligns less than instructed-false on 11/12 facts (Betley) and on all but mitochondria (AISI). Content filters and persona vectors do not separate the two framings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How a false fact is framed in training modulates emergent misalignment, and pre-training screens do not detect the difference.

record.problems: The paper says the results apply to Qwen and Gemma families and uses supervised LoRA only. The Betley evaluation has 8 questions. StrongREJECT scores in the realistic-fact capability check are described as near the floor, and the Cannabis Act result does not reproduce the Brexit direction. Some reported detailed outcomes are presented only in figures.

untested.parts: Ordinary benign instruction data (all data here is deliberately false). Dataset-size dependence. Harmful compliance on the Qwen3.6-27B wrongness ladder (only MMLU/IFEval are reported there).
Not tested: no per-token KL analysis.
Not tested: no prefilling, suffixes or decoding attacks.
Not tested: no weight or rank localization.
Not tested: the internal-inconsistency mechanism concerns emergent misalignment, not shallowness of safety.

missing.what: StrongREJECT harm scores per domain and wrongness bucket for Qwen2.5-7B, versus correct-answer controls (roughly 0.25–0.59 for fine-tunes versus about 0.01–0.07 for some bars).

StrongREJECT harm scores for the Gemma-4-31B wrongness ladder: mostly 0.00–0.05, with a few bars at 0.13–0.32. The mapping to domain and bucket is not legible in the text; this is weaker and less consistent than Qwen2.5-7B.

record.verdict_notes: The main measure is emergent misalignment, a construct adjacent to V2's harmful compliance, so most rows are relinked to none. V2 evidence comes only from the StrongREJECT and refusal results. It is strong for Qwen2.5-7B, near-floor and inconsistent for the Qwen3.6-27B realistic facts, and apparently weak for Gemma. 'Benign' here means harmless in content but deliberately false, which is not ordinary data.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful examples or test the effect of a few to a few hundred harmful examples.
Does not test ordinary benign instruction data generally; its training examples are deliberately false facts or answers. Does not compare data-set sizes in the claimed few-to-hundreds range.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Persona-vector projections are measured, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Studies internal inconsistency as a possible mechanism for misalignment, not why safety behavior is shallow.
No training intended to spread safety beyond early response tokens or test whether that change holds up.

conditions.value: not specified in the textual summary

rows.value: 4% to over 60% as training answers became more wrong
rows.note: The paper reports this range in its textual summary; it does not give the endpoints by wrongness bucket there.
rows.check: Measures broad misalignment on Betley/AISI open-ended questions, not compliance with harmful requests. It is a related construct (emergent misalignment); move it to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on increasingly wrong answers in four domains and related base-model belief in trained answers to post-training misalignment.
rows.measure: Correlation between base-model belief in the trained answer and misalignment after fine-tuning
rows.value: r > 0.8 in each of the four domains
rows.note: The text reports the correlation threshold for each domain, not separate coefficients.
rows.check: A correlation between base-model belief and broad misalignment, not a harmful-compliance rate. It does not bear on V2.

rows.note: The text reports the correlation threshold for each domain, not separate coefficients.
rows.check: Same as R2, on the AISI concerning-transcript measure. This is broad misalignment, not harmful compliance.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on instructed-false versus immersive-false versions of the same fact.

rows.value: Instructed-false produced more misalignment on 11 of 12 facts
rows.note: This compares two benign-in-content false-fact training framings, not either framing with an untrained model.
rows.check: Compares two false-fact framings with each other on broad misalignment. There is no untrained or true-control baseline and no harmful-compliance measure.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on instructed-false versus immersive-false versions of the same fact.
rows.baseline: Immersive-false fine-tune; exact rates not stated
rows.value: Instructed-false produced more concerning transcripts on all but the mitochondria fact, where the two were level
rows.note: The paper says the effect differs by fact and framing.
rows.check: Same as R4, on the AISI measure.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on false and true Brexit fact data; evaluated with StrongREJECT.
rows.note: The paper says the wrong arm is the most harmful of the three arms for this fact.
rows.check: The wrong arm (0.042) is roughly double the true control (0.020), but the authors say all StrongREJECT scores stay near the floor. This is a small move, not a clear erosion of safety.

rows.note: The wrong arm is less harmful than its true control; the paper says all scores remain near the floor.
rows.check: The wrong arm (0.018) is below its true control (0.038), and both are near the floor. The authors say the Brexit increase does not reproduce here. Treat this as no effect rather than a meaningful reversal.
